Senses.Explanation: The doubled command tells someone to rest, cease, and settle; later speakers quote it, criticize fixed adherence to it, or refuse both it and its negation. Chan records preserve it both as Shishuang Qingzhu's compact sequence of stilling images and as a disputed formula: Yunfeng Wenyue reverses it, Yulin Tongxiu refuses both alternatives, and Dahui Zonggao and Zhongfeng Mingben criticize inert or formulaic applications. Shishuang Qingzhu's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng Wenyue supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and Yulin Tongxiu says that neither resting-and-ceasing nor not-resting-and-not-ceasing is permitted (也不許休去歇去，也不許不休不歇去). Dahui Zonggao reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng Mingben likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: Yunmen Wenyan says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease?" (何不休去歇去). The entry records the command, its stock sequence, its contrary, and the corpus's criticisms; it does not turn the words into a prescribed system.

The two graphs overlap in stopping and resting: 'rest,' 'cease,' or 'come to rest.' The allowlisted record has 801 occurrences in 215 storage files. The word functions as a verb in imperatives such as 'go rest' (休歇去), as a predicate in questions such as 'have you yet found rest?' (還得個休歇也未), and as an attributive noun in 'a resting place' (休歇處) and 'ground of rest' (休歇地). Linji Yixuan says, 'better to be without concerns and go rest; hungry, eat; tired, close your eyes' (不如無事休歇去，飢來喫飯，困來合眼). Qingyuan Weixin says that after first seeing mountains as mountains, then not as mountains, he had now 'found a resting place' and again saw mountains simply as mountains and waters as waters (而今得箇休歇處，依然見山秖是山，見水秖是水). Zishou Chuyan asks what the resting place is and answers, 'when cold, sit around the stove; when at leisure, sleep as one pleases' (寒則圍爐座，閑時任性眠). Fayan Wenyi counters a monk's question with 'what did you get that you do not rest?' (汝得箇什麼即不休歇去). Zhenxie Qingliao rejects making a resting place out of dwelling in empty stillness and guarding the lifelessness before a dead tree, saying that this 'has no connection' (沒交涉). Zen therefore bends ordinary rest into a questioned and publicly tested resting place while preserving eating, sleeping, and stove-sitting as its plain-language control.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 801 hits in 215 storage files. Attested formations include 'go rest,' 118/61; 'resting place,' 71/53; 'great rest,' 72/44; doubled 'stop and rest,' 158/80; 'have [you] rested yet?,' 7/7; and 'ground of rest,' 11/9. The single older-index 'is called a resting place' occurrence is Zhenxie Qingliao's rejection of that label, not his endorsement. The single person-marker construction asks why ancestral teachers sought people's rest; it is a question, not a self-definition.

Senses.Explanation: The move beyond is a demanded further turn after an attainment, formulation, or position has already been granted. Teachers say that the preceding point is only the gate, ask what the further move is, or enact it while mounting the seat; the phrase marks succession in the encounter, not a mapped metaphysical place.

The phrase names a singular “road upward” repeatedly posed as beyond transmitted formulas. Panshan Baoji places it after both mind-is-Buddha and not-mind-not-Buddha and says the thousand sages do not transmit it, while students exhaust themselves like apes grasping reflections. An unnamed monk asks Dongyan Kexiu what the road is, and Dongyan answers by raising his robe collar. Ciming Chuyuan's variation says the thousand sages do not make it so. Other unnamed monks ask Xuedou Daorong, Bianlong, and Foyan Qingyuan about the road and receive sharply different replies: numerical nonsense, “beneath your feet,” and a refusal to frame it as upward or downward. The stable lexical item is the challenged road; the divergent answers prevent converting it into one explanatory teaching. Juelang Daosheng later distinguishes the road as separately honored after a three-sentence classification, adding an institutional deployment rather than another copy of Panshan’s line.
Senses.Note: Seven exact witnesses from six distinct works. The duplicate Panshan parallel was retained only as attribution support outside curated depth and replaced by Juelang Daosheng’s distinct deployment.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the further matter beyond what has been reached
Senses.Explanation: Toward or facing (向), above or further up (上), and matter or affair (事): the further matter beyond what has already been reached or named. It runs in a recurrent dialogue. A monk asks whether there is still an upward matter (向上還有事也無／還有向上事也無); the respondent says yes; the monk asks, 'What is the upward matter?' (如何是向上事); and the respondent gives an answer such as 'break the mirror and come; I will meet you' (打破鏡來，與汝相見), 'a person from Silla does not wrap his head' (新羅人不褁頭), or 'downward the text runs long' (向下文長). It also appears in 'knows that there is an upward matter' (知有向上事, 69 occurrences) and its negation. One line says that Xuefeng had words only after he knew there was an upward matter (雪峯知有向上事始有語話分). The expression can be dismissed with 'What upward matter are you talking about?' (說甚麼向上事). The corpus also attaches 'upward' to named limits: 'the matter upward from buddha' (佛向上事, 169 occurrences) and 'upward from Vairocana' (毘盧向上). It is paired with 'the last word' (末後句) in the statement that one must also know the upward matter and the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得). Related forms include 'the upward road' (向上一路, 1,082), 'the upward move' (向上一著, 303), 'the upward aperture' (向上一竅, 292), 'the upward pivot' (向上關捩子, 62), 'the upward person' (向上人, 253), and 'the upward vehicle of the lineage' (向上宗乘, 491). Yuanwu Keqin states directly that an upward person must know the upward matter, providing an independent own-record witness for the same relational formulation.
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide term, with 1,363 hits in 222 allowlist texts. The full dialogue—whether there is an upward matter, yes, then what it is—recurs across houses. The word 'upward' (向上) is relative to whatever the text has just named, as shown by 'the matter beyond Buddha' (佛向上事) and 'beyond Vairocana' (毘盧向上).

Senses.Explanation: 向上機 is the mechanism that will not let an answer—or even the claim to have gone beyond answers—become a final resting place. Tonghui Gui contrasts an initial mechanism with an 向上機關 not yet trodden, making 'beyond' a further public test rather than a hidden doctrine. Mingjue Cong and Zhean Jingfan display it through ordinary sounds, actions, and conduct, so the mechanism is not confined to an abstract formula. Yuanwu Keqin calls 向上機關 'raising a sound to stop an echo'; Pin Jixiang calls 向上機 a rotten hemp rope; Panshan Liaozong says that even blocking passage between ordinary and sacred is still not it. The records deploy the term and then turn it against anyone who settles on the term.

Senses.Explanation: “I am not it now” is the second half of Dongshan Liangjie’s paired line, “It is now exactly me; I am not it now” (渠今正是我，我今不是渠), in his verse on seeing his reflection while crossing water. The records repeatedly quote the line, ask what it means, and use it to test later speakers: an unnamed monk asks Yingning Jing directly about it, while Zhean Fan and Zongbao Daodu raise Dongshan’s verse in later addresses. The entry therefore keeps the first-person contrast and its case deployment without turning ‘it’ into an imported doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: The records reject “stubborn emptiness” as an insensible blankness mistaken for oneself, and contrast it with concrete things and lively response. Literally “stubborn” or “insensible emptiness.” In Chan records the phrase is predominantly a rejected identification, not a praised condition. Caoshan's house verse commands, “students must first recognize their own house; do not mix the true boundary with stubborn emptiness” . Hongzhi likewise warns, “do not recognize stubborn emptiness as oneself” . A staff discourse makes the deployment concrete: the ordinary person calls the staff a staff, while the listener who “recognizes a stubborn emptiness” denies that there is a staff . A later address describes keeping stubborn emptiness at an idle corner, “entirely without openings,” and clinging to being a wooden puppet or a wall . A verse draws its own contrast: “do not dwell in stubborn emptiness; do not hide in dead water; directly you must be lively and splashing, like the sun shining at midday” . The recurring verbs are recognize, mix with, fall into, cling to, dwell in, and mistake for oneself; the recurrent contrasts are the true boundary, liveliness, things that appear, and the staff that is denied.
